blocks.text: A cement plant in Sokoto needs to know exactly how much limestone to feed into the kiln to produce one tonne of quicklime. Order too little and production stops; order too much and money sits idle. The calculation that answers the question is the same one you will meet in the exam, only with bigger numbers.

blocks.markdown:
## The balanced equation is a mole recipe

A balanced equation does not tell you about grams. It tells you about **moles**.

CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2

read as: *one mole of calcium carbonate gives one mole of calcium oxide and one mole of carbon dioxide*.

For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, the ratio is two moles of magnesium to one mole of oxygen molecules to two moles of magnesium oxide.

blocks.title: The three-step route
blocks.text: Every reacting-mass problem follows the same path. Step 1: convert the known mass to moles using n = m / M. Step 2: use the mole ratio from the balanced equation to find the moles of the required substance. Step 3: convert those moles back to mass, volume or concentration. Never try to use a mass ratio directly.

blocks.markdown:
### Balancing first

A calculation built on an unbalanced equation is worthless, so balance before anything else.

Balance metals first, then non-metals other than hydrogen and oxygen, then hydrogen, and oxygen last. For the combustion of propane:

C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O

Three carbons fix the CO2 coefficient at 3, eight hydrogens fix H2O at 4, and the right-hand side then has 6 + 4 = 10 oxygen atoms, requiring 5 O2.

blocks.title: Mass of product from a given mass of reactant
blocks.prompt: Calculate the mass of calcium oxide produced when 25 g of calcium carbonate is completely decomposed by heating. [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16]

steps.text: Write the balanced equation. CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. All coefficients are 1, so the mole ratio of CaCO3 to CaO is 1 : 1.
Find the molar mass of the known substance. M(CaCO3) = 40 + 12 + (3 x 16) = 100 g/mol.
Convert the given mass to moles.
Apply the mole ratio. Since CaCO3 : CaO is 1 : 1, moles of CaO = 0.25 mol.
Find the molar mass of the product. M(CaO) = 40 + 16 = 56 g/mol.
Check by conservation of mass: 25 g of CaCO3 gives 14 g of CaO plus 0.25 x 44 = 11 g of CO2, and 14 + 11 = 25 g. Correct.

blocks.title: Limiting reactant and volume of gas
blocks.prompt: 10 g of calcium carbonate is added to 100 cm3 of 1.0 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. Which reactant is limiting, and what volume of carbon dioxide is produced at s.t.p.? [Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16; molar volume at s.t.p. = 22.4 dm3/mol]

steps.text: Balanced equation: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The mole ratio of CaCO3 to HCl is 1 : 2.
Moles of HCl = concentration x volume in dm3 = 1.0 x 0.100 = 0.10 mol.
Compare with the ratio. Reacting all 0.10 mol of CaCO3 would need 0.20 mol of HCl, but only 0.10 mol is available, so the acid runs out first. HCl is the limiting reactant.
Base the calculation on HCl. From the ratio 2HCl : 1CO2, moles of CO2 = 0.10 / 2 = 0.050 mol.

blocks.answer: Hydrochloric acid is limiting; 1.12 dm3 of carbon dioxide is produced at s.t.p.

blocks.title: Percentage yield
blocks.text: Percentage yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical mass calculated from the equation, multiplied by 100. Real yields fall short because reactions may be reversible, side reactions occur and some product is lost during transfer and purification.

blocks.title: Two habits that protect your marks
blocks.text: First, always check that the equation is balanced before using any ratio. Second, quote units at every stage — mol, g, dm3 — because a missing unit costs a mark even when the number is right.

points: A balanced equation gives the ratio in moles, never in grams.
Convert the given quantity to moles, apply the mole ratio, then convert back.
The limiting reactant is the one that would run out first; it fixes the amount of product.
Volume of a gas at s.t.p. equals the number of moles multiplied by 22.4 dm3.
Percentage yield is actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
